cells.tense: The pen is in your hand and the thinking is moving clean.
cells.ask: Pick one piece you've refined and put it in front of one person today. Not for notes — so it exists outside the room you made it in.
cells.core:
A tangle of a problem opens under your hand and the one true line through it shows up fast. The speed isn't a trick. It comes from having done this slowly, by yourself, many times, and those hours are what make the move that quick.

What comes next is quieter than another round at the desk. The shine belongs to work that finished; it isn't yours to paint on top of it. So put one piece where another pair of eyes can land. Send the draft, set the pattern on the table, let the reading be heard. Then stop, and see what the work does once it's standing on its own.
cells.sheetLine: The work is done enough. Let one piece be seen.
cells.verb: Cutting through to what is logically true, and putting it to use.
cells.place: In a practice room, refining one skill by repeated attention.

cells.tense: You're bracing at a room that hasn't happened yet, answering early.
cells.ask: Leave an unfinished draft alone for a week. Add nothing, fix nothing. If your hand goes toward a sentence, note the impulse and stop there.
cells.core:
The cut can serve the thing it was made for. You find the true line, then let the work sit and speak for itself — clear enough that another person can follow it at their own speed, without being outrun. Structure that serves what it organizes: steady, legible, no argument needed.

The trouble is that the cut now runs ahead of the work. The answer arrives before the question does, so the room gets pre-empted instead of entered. You're revising against a future where it's already understood, and paying for that future now. The rush is taking what the rush was for. Set one draft down for seven days and hear what it says without you.
cells.sheetLine: You're answering questions nobody has asked yet.

cells.tense: The thinking went quiet a while back and you're still at the door.
cells.ask: Take the smallest piece of this practice and do it in front of one other person this week. Don't explain it first — just work while they are present.
cells.core:
When this seat is running well, the sharp thinking moves out of the head and into a room. You take a thing worked out alone and hand it over — teach it, work it through with someone watching, let it land in another head and shift there. What you know stays yours, and it gets clearer with a listener on the other side of it.

The practice has gone private and stayed private. Refining still happens on its own; the handing-over is what stopped. So don't push for more effort into the practice itself. Pick the smallest thing you're already steady at and do it with one person nearby. Teaching that adapts, said out loud, pulls the current back through — not another solo hour.

cells.tense: You're already seeing the shape and calling it just how things are.
cells.ask: Say out loud once, to one person: 'Here's what I make of this.' Take one read you've been treating as obvious and put your name on it.
cells.core:
Spotting the pattern and saying you spot it can be one motion. You catch the real shape of a problem, then tell the person across from you what you make of it — plain enough that both of you can move on it. The notice does its work, and the person hearing it gets to be a peer, not an audience.

What runs instead is the read with no author attached. The pattern lands before anyone finishes the sentence, and it gets reported like the temperature. So do the simpler move underneath: name it as yours, once. The person you tell doesn't need a stage. They need your hand on the sentence. 'Here's what I make of this,' said to one person today.
cells.sheetLine: You see it clearly. Say the reading out loud as yours.
